headline_marked: [[Cloud Resume Challenge]] Completed: Serverless Backend Built From Scratch
headline: Cloud Resume Challenge Completed: Serverless Backend Built From Scratch
summary: An IT student details their journey building a secure, automated serverless backend for the Azure Cloud Resume Challenge, leveraging AI coding tools.
details: An IT student embarking on their third year has successfully completed the Azure Cloud Resume Challenge, architecting a secure, fully automated serverless backend from scratch. This project aimed to bridge the gap between theoretical cloud knowledge and practical, production-ready infrastructure deployment.

The student utilized AI coding tools as a pair-programmer, focusing on high-level engineering tasks such as orchestrating automation and debugging remote cloud conflicts, rather than getting bogged down in syntax. This 'agentic' workflow accelerated the development process.

The project involved passing the Microsoft AZ-900 exam for foundational Azure knowledge, designing a custom HTML/CSS aesthetic with an Azure color palette, and hosting a static frontend on Azure Blob Storage with custom domain mapping and HTTPS enforcement via Cloudflare.

A lightweight JavaScript client was implemented to display a live visitor count by automatically querying the backend database on page load. The serverless backend itself uses Azure Cosmos DB (Table API) for data storage and an Azure Functions Python v2 API for retrieving and updating visitor counts.

Automated unit tests were written using pytest to ensure code reliability before cloud deployment, and Infrastructure as Code (IaC) was employed using an Azure Bicep template to automate the creation of the database, storage account, and function app.

Challenges encountered included Azure initially injecting an incorrect SQL-formatted connection string, which was resolved by correcting the Bicep template. Additionally, backend deployment errors (503) were fixed by removing a conflicting read-only setting in the Bicep template that interfered with GitHub Actions' remote build process.

The project was fully automated using GitHub Actions for both backend and frontend deployments, ensuring that code pushes trigger automatic testing and deployment to Azure. The completed project serves as a live demonstration of the student's ability to design, test, deploy, and secure cloud infrastructure.

headline_marked: [[Video Game Data]] to Train AI World Models, Startup Claims
headline: Video Game Data to Train AI World Models, Startup Claims
summary: A British startup is packaging controller inputs and other data from video games to train artificial intelligence models, aiming to solve the shortage of real-world training data.
details: A British startup, Worldmodeldata, is aiming to solve a critical data shortage for training AI 'world models' by using data from video games. These models need to understand physics and real-world interactions, which are difficult to capture with text-based data alone.

Worldmodeldata believes that the visual representations and player actions found in video games provide a vast, abundant, and diverse source of training material. They are acting as a broker, curating and organizing this data from game studios for AI labs.

The startup claims to have licensed nearly 1 million hours of data from popular video game studios, though specific names were not disclosed. This data includes controller inputs and visual environments, which are crucial for teaching AI cause and consequence.

This approach could potentially lead to a 'GPT moment' for world models, making them significantly more useful for tasks like piloting autonomous vehicles, operating robotic arms, or controlling drones. The cost of error in these real-world applications is very high.

While some researchers and companies like General Intuition and Niantic are already collecting their own game data, Worldmodeldata aims to simplify the process by offering a centralized, curated dataset. They also plan to compensate individual players in the future.

However, not all industry players are convinced. Nvidia, a leader in AI hardware and world model development, prefers to use its custom engine designed to replicate real-world physics, suggesting that video game inputs might not be sufficient for robust training.
